props.title: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein

sections.content: Kenneth Branagh's ambitious Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1994) stands as the most faithful adaptation of Shelley's gothic novel, embracing both its philosophical weight and romantic elements. Unlike the iconic Universal monster movie Frankenstein (1931), Branagh's version dives deep into Victor Frankenstein's hubris and the creature's tragic humanity. Robert De Niro's scarred, eloquent creature shares more DNA with Shelley's original creation than Boris Karloff's grunting monster, while Branagh's feverish direction mirrors the novel's romantic excess.

sections.content: The creature's cinematic evolution reflects changing attitudes toward science and human responsibility. Young Frankenstein (1974) brilliantly parodies Universal's monster while honoring its imagery. Frankenstein Unbound (1990) merges sci-fi with biography, placing Mary Shelley herself within a time-travel narrative. Even I, Frankenstein (2014), despite its action-heavy approach, grapples with the creature's search for identity and purpose. SUBHEAD: Gothic Horror and Scientific Ethics

Modern Frankenstein adaptations increasingly emphasize bioethical questions. Ex Machina (2014) and Blade Runner (1982) inherit Shelley's concerns about creating artificial life, while Splice (2009) directly confronts genetic engineering's moral implications. The Fly (1986) echoes Frankenstein's themes of scientific ambition leading to physical transformation and inevitable tragedy.
